## Icon

When building modern dashboards, using Iconify is tempting because of its massive catalog (150,000+ icons from Solar, Lucide, Tabler, Carbon, etc.). However, **how** you load them matters.

Many templates use `@iconify/react` (e.g., `<Icon icon="solar:user-bold" />`). While convenient, this streams icon SVGs at runtime from an external CDN (`api.iconify.design`):

- **Flash of Unstyled Icons (FOIC)**: Icons pop in with a delay after the page loads, causing visual layout shifts (CLS).
- **Network & Offline Failures**: If the user has a spotty connection, is offline, or runs behind a strict corporate firewall, icons simply fail to render.
- **Runtime Overhead**: Requires an extra client-side parser and continuous HTTP requests.

Z3 Admin bundles icons at compile time via Vite:

1. **Centralized Common Icons**: Repeated icons (`SearchIcon`, `CloseIcon`, `ChevronDownIcon`, `UserIcon`) are consolidated in [`packages/core/src/components/ui/icons.tsx`](file:///Users/leonhong/Personal%20Project/admin-template/packages/core/src/components/ui/icons.tsx) and exported via `@z3/admin-core`:

```tsx
import { SearchIcon, CloseIcon, Icons } from "@z3/admin-core";
```

2. **Feature-Specific Icons**: When you need a one-off icon for a specific feature, import it directly on the fly:

```tsx
import DashboardIcon from "~icons/solar/widget-5-bold";
import CartIcon from "~icons/solar/cart-4-bold";
```

Better Auth integration, session management, role permissions, and TOTP two-factor authentication.

Auth is what makes or breaks an application. No matter how great your UI or features are, if you cannot protect your users from unauthorized access, everything else falls apart. This is more relevant than ever in the age of AI. When anyone can prompt an application into existence out of thin air, security is often the first thing neglected. To build software that actually lasts in production, you have to understand its fundamentals. ## Core Concept HTTP is stateless by default, When you make a request, the server treats every incoming request as if it has never seen the client before, but not all request are equal, some routes are public, some require a logged-in user, and some are restricted to admin. That is where the concept of **Authentication** and **Authorization** come in. ### What is Authentication? Authentication is the process of verifying identity. In web applications, this usually boils down to two transport strategies: - **HTTP-Only Cookies (Session-Based)**: After login, the server sets a cookie containing a session ID. Browsers automatically attach this cookie to subsequent requests. Because the cookie is marked **HttpOnly**, client-side JavaScript cannot access it via `document.cookie`, making it immune to token theft via XSS attacks. The trade-off is that it requires proper CORS configuration (`credentials: "include"` on the client and explicit origins on the backend) and protection against CSRF. - **Bearer Tokens (JWT / State Storage)**: After login, the server returns an access token that the client stores in memory or `localStorage` and attaches manually via the `Authorization: Bearer ` header. This is convenient for mobile apps and third-party APIs. However, tokens stored in `localStorage` are vulnerable to XSS. Standard mitigation is issuing short-lived access tokens (e.g., 10 minutes) paired with a refresh token to rotate credentials frequently. ### What is Authorization? Once a user proves who they are, authorization determines what they can touch. Even after successful login, regular users shouldn't access billing settings or manage user accounts. that's why we need to also define clear **Permission**. For example, only user with role `admin` can create new user, or only `admin` can promote user to `admin`, etc. ### Common Misconception You'll often hear: "Never roll your own auth." For production apps, that's sound advice, hashing passwords, handling session revocation, and mitigating timing attacks are easy to get wrong. But as a learning exercise, building auth from scratch at least once is invaluable. you will understand how cookies, salt/hash algorithms, and sessions work under the hood. For Z3 Admin, we chose Better Auth. Unlike NextAuth/Auth.js (which is tightly coupled to Next.js), Better Auth is framework-agnostic, built for TypeScript, integrates cleanly and provides modular plugins like TOTP, role-based permissions right out of the box. ## 2FA Authentication Email and password is often never truly enough to protect you from getting your identity stolen. That is why is second layer of protection is crucial for most application nowaday. There are many methods, noticably OTP (One Time Password), TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password), and Passkeys. - **OTP**: Once you login, the server will send a random passphrase to either the user email or phone number, only after type in the correct passphrase Better Auth's Two-Factor plugin is fully wired from database to UI: 1. **Password Verification**: User confirms password to initiate 2FA setup. 2. **QR Code Generation**: Displays SVG QR code generated with `react-qr-code` and plain base32 secret. 3. **6-Digit Challenge**: User inputs TOTP authenticator code to enable 2FA. 4. **Backup Recovery Codes**: Modal provides 10 single-use emergency backup recovery codes downloadable as `.txt` or copyable. 5. **Challenge on Login**: Unauthenticated login detects `TWO_FACTOR_REDIRECT` and presents the 6-digit TOTP challenge screen. ## Frontend Auth Hook ```tsx import { useAuth } from "@z3/admin-core"; export function UserHeader() { const { user, isAuthenticated, signOut } = useAuth(); return (
Welcome, {user?.name} ({user?.role})
); } ```
TanStack Router file-based routing, type-safe search params, route guards, and nested navigation.

When choosing a router for modern React, the two main contenders are React Router and TanStack Router. I ultimately chose [TanStack Router](https://tanstack.com/router/latest) with file-based route generation for its end-to-end type safety and built-in search param validation.

## Why File-Based Routing?

I initially leaned toward code-based routing. However, after testing both approaches, file-based routing proved far more maintainable. Unless your project is extremely complex with deep level routing, the convenience trade off is just not worth it.
Another factor is our sidebar navigation. Having to define routes manually in code and then turn around to configure the sidebar separately felt like out-of-sync paths. File-based keeps everything intuitive and centralized. You can just focus on the feature instead of going back and forth with defining route.
That said, don't feel locked in. If you ever need fine-grained control, you can always swap back to a code-based setup by checking out the [TanStack Router Dpcs](https://tanstack.com/router/latest/docs/installation/manual#using-code-based-route-configuration).

---

## Route Hierarchy & Thin Route Files

`apps/starter` uses TanStack Router's pathless layout route (`_authenticated.tsx`) to guard private pages and wrap them in `<AdminLayout>`:

```zsh
apps/starter/src/routes/
├── __root.tsx                    # Root HTML container and QueryClient provider
├── login.tsx                     # Public unauthenticated login route (/login)
└── _authenticated.tsx            # Authenticated layout guard (wraps AdminLayout)
    └── _authenticated/
        ├── index.tsx             # Dashboard (/)
        ├── shop/
        │   ├── products.tsx      # Products (/shop/products)
        │   └── orders.tsx        # Orders (/shop/orders)
        ├── users.tsx             # Users (/users)
        └── settings.tsx          # Settings & 2FA (/settings)
```

### Thin Routes & Module Colocation

Route files in `src/routes/` are intentionally **thin** (often under 10 lines). Route files should focus strictly on routing, search param validation, and loader context—while all UI, state, and feature components live in `src/modules/`:

```zsh
src/
├── modules/user/                 # Feature module (domain logic)
│   ├── api/user.api.ts           # React Query hooks
│   ├── components/               # Feature-specific modals & column defs
│   │   ├── change-role-modal.tsx
│   │   └── user.column.tsx
│   └── user.page.tsx             # Main view component
└── routes/_authenticated/
    └── users.tsx                 # Thin route entrypoint
```

Here is the entire [`users.tsx`](file:///Users/leonhong/Personal%20Project/admin-template/apps/starter/src/routes/_authenticated/users.tsx) route file:

```tsx
import { createFileRoute } from "@tanstack/react-router";
import { UserPage } from "../../modules/user/user.page";
import { ListUsersQuerySchema, safeValidateSearch } from "@z3/types";

export const Route = createFileRoute("/_authenticated/users")({
  // Type-safe URL search params validated against shared Valibot schema
  validateSearch: safeValidateSearch(ListUsersQuerySchema),
  component: UserPage,
});
```

## Route Guards (`beforeLoad`)

Protected routes check user authentication inside `_authenticated.tsx` via TanStack Router's `beforeLoad` hook:

```tsx
export const Route = createFileRoute("/_authenticated")({
  beforeLoad: ({ context, location }) => {
    if (!context.auth.isLoading && !context.auth.isAuthenticated) {
      throw redirect({
        to: "/login",
        search: { redirect: location.href },
      });
    }
  },
  component: AuthenticatedLayout,
  notFoundComponent: AuthenticatedNotFound,
});
```

Z3 Admin is structured as a Turborepo monorepo managed with Bun workspaces.

```zsh
z3-admin/

│   ├── starter/           # React 19 + TanStack Router frontend client
│   ├── backend/           # Express 5 + Drizzle ORM + Better Auth backend API

├── packages/
│   ├── core/              # Core framework, UI components, layout, styling (@z3/admin-core)
│   ├── types/             # Shared Valibot schemas & TypeScript models (@z3/types)
│   ├── eslint-config/     # Shared ESLint configuration (@z3/eslint-config)
│   └── typescript-config/ # Shared TypeScript base configs (@z3/typescript-config)
├── docker-compose.yml     # Local PostgreSQL 16 container definition
└── package.json           # Monorepo root scripts & workspace configuration
```

## Feature Based Architecture

Z3 Admin enforces feature-based colocation across both frontend and backend rather than grouping by technical file types (e.g., throwing all components or controllers into single massive global folders).

```zsh
z3-admin/
├── apps/
│   ├── starter/src/modules/
│   │   └── order/
│   │       ├── api/
│   │       │   └── order.api.ts          # TanStack Query & mutation hooks
│   │       ├── components/
│   │       │   ├── order-modal.tsx       # Feature-specific modals/drawers
│   │       │   └── order.column.tsx      # DataTable column definitions
│   │       └── order.page.tsx            # Main page view component
│   └── backend/src/modules/
│       └── order/
│           ├── order.route.ts            # Route definitions & guards
│           ├── order.controller.ts       # HTTP request parsing & response handling
│           ├── order.service.ts          # Core business logic
│           └── order.repository.ts       # Direct database queries (Drizzle ORM)
```

### Why Feature Colocation?

When building real-world project, features grow quickly. Isolating each domain (such as `order`, `product`, or `user`) into its own folder keeps the codebase modular and readable:

- Isolated blast radius: If order checkout breaks, all relevant UI, queries, API endpoints, and database queries live in the order/ directory.
- Easy deletion & refactoring: When a feature is deprecated or reworked, removing its module folder cleanly deletes 90% of its related code without hunting through scattered root folders.

## Backend Architecture

```zsh
z3-admin/
├── apps/
│   ├── backend/
│     └── modules/
│       └── orders/
│           └── order.repository.ts
│           └── order.service.ts
│           └── order.controller.ts
│           └── order.route.ts
```

After battling and changing pattern multiple times, I ultimately decided to follows Controller-Service-Repository layered architecture (inspired by NestJS and Clean Architecture principles):

- **Route (`*.route.ts`)**: Defines HTTP verbs, paths, and attaches route-level middlewares.
- **Controller (`*.controller.ts`)**: Extracts request params/body, input validation, execute service function.
- **Service (`*.service.ts`)**: Houses pure business logic, permissions, validations, and multi-step workflows.
- **Repository (`*.repository.ts`)**: The only layer that touches Drizzle ORM and executes direct database queries. If you change your ORM or database engine, only this layer changes.

Instead of writing separate frontend and backend TypeScript types (which quickly get out of sync), we place all application domain, and types in `packages/type`.

Overview of Z3 Admin features, philosophy, and tech stack.

**Z3 Admin** is a personal project born out of years of building real-world admin applications, distilling those lessons into a clean, modern monorepo setup.

## Why This Exists

Every time I started a new admin dashboard, I found myself repeatedly solving the same problems from scratch: setting up table pagination, wiring auth sessions, handling modals on mobile screens, or copying messy utility snippets between repositories.

I built **Z3 Admin** to solve two goals:

1. **A Ready-to-Use Foundation**: A production-grade starter you can clone or scaffold with a single command to get building immediately.
2. **An Architectural Reference & Learning Resource**: A transparent look into modern fullstack architecture. Beyond code to copy, this repository and documentation serve as a playbook explaining **why** specific technical choices were made—from monorepo boundary separation and compound component design to choosing Valibot and TanStack Router.
   Whether you're looking to launch a new dashboard or studying how to architect a modern TypeScript monorepo, everything here is built to be read, learned from, and extended.

## Key Principles

1. **Don't Reinvent the Wheel**: UI components (`DataTable`, `Select`, `Modal`, `Drawer`, `WorkspaceTabs`) live centrally in `@z3/admin-core` to prevent fragmented, copy-pasted UI logic across features.
2. **Mobile Friendly**: Admin dashboards should be fully usable on phones and tablets, not just ultra-wide monitors. Every layout and modal is responsive by default.
3. **End-to-End Type Safety & DX**: Valibot schemas (`@z3/types`) shared across frontend and backend, strict file-based routing, zero scattered helper files, and machine-readable docs (`/llms.txt`).
4. **Plug & Play / Modular**: Run with mock data out of the box for instant UI work, or spin up the full Express 5 + PostgreSQL backend with a single setup command.

## Technology Used

| Layer                 | Technology                                                       |
| :-------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Package Manager**   | [Bun](https://bun.sh) (with `workspace:*` dependency protocol)   |
| **Monorepo Engine**   | [Turborepo](https://turbo.build)                                 |
| **Frontend**          | React 19, Vite, TanStack Router, TanStack Query, Tailwind CSS v4 |
| **Backend**           | Express, Drizzle ORM, PostgreSQL, Better Auth, Scalar Docs       |
| **Core UI Library**   | Headless UI v2, Iconify (`unplugin-icons`)                       |
| **Schema Validation** | [Valibot](https://valibot.dev) (shared across client and server) |

## Future Plan

This project isn't meant to stay locked into a single stack. Good architecture doesn't start and stop with React + Express—there are plenty of great tools worth exploring.

When time permits, I'd love to expand support to alternatives like **Vue / Nuxt** on the frontend, or **Hono / Elysia** on the backend.

If you have ideas or want to help add new adapters, PRs and discussions are always welcome!

## Custom Hooks

### `useQueryFilters` / `useTableFilters`
Synchronizes search input and dropdown filters with URL search parameters:

```tsx
const {
  filters,
  searchValue,
  setSearchValue,
  setFilter,
  resetFilters,
  isFiltered,
} = useQueryFilters({
  defaultValues: { search: "", role: "all" },
});
```
